title: Message Queues
subtitle: Watch a checkout hand work to a queue, survive a traffic spike and a worker crash, and park a poison message.
learn: How a queue decouples producers from consumers and absorbs bursts
What at-least-once delivery means and why duplicates happen
How acknowledgements and the visibility timeout recover from crashed workers
What a dead-letter queue is for and when messages end up there

steps.title: Don't make checkout wait
steps.body: After a purchase, the checkout service must email a receipt. If checkout calls the email provider directly, the customer waits for that call (often 300 ms to 2 s). Worse, if the provider is down, the order fails just because of an email. But a receipt can arrive a few seconds later. So why should checkout wait for it?
steps.idea: Work that does not need to finish before you reply should not hold up the reply.
steps.caption: Checkout is tied to the slow email provider.

steps.title: Hand the job to a queue
steps.body: Instead, checkout writes a small message such as 'send receipt for order 81' to a queue. The queue confirms it has stored the message, usually within a few milliseconds. The service that writes the message is the producer. Checkout can now reply to the customer right away, even if no email worker is running. Think of the queue as a to-do tray: the producer drops a note in, and workers pick notes up when they are free.
steps.idea: A queue keeps messages (durably, if set to persist) until a worker is ready to handle them.
steps.caption: Checkout drops a message in the queue and gets 'stored'.

steps.title: Absorb a spike
steps.body: A flash sale sends 300 orders per second for 10 seconds: 3,000 messages. Assume each worker sends about 40 emails per second, so two workers manage 80 per second. In 10 seconds they send 800, so about 2,200 messages are left waiting. At 80 per second the backlog drains in about 27 s, roughly half a minute. Without the queue, checkout would have to wait on, or fail against, an email system sized for 300 per second.
steps.idea: A queue turns a short burst into a longer, steady flow that the workers can handle.
steps.caption: Depth climbs during the burst, then drains.

steps.title: Receive hides the message
steps.body: Worker A asks the queue for a message. The queue does not delete it. It hides it from other workers for a set time, called the visibility timeout (30 seconds here), and counts one delivery attempt. The message is lent to Worker A, not given away. Meanwhile Worker B receives different messages, so the work is shared. In the HUD, one message moves from waiting to in flight.
steps.idea: Receiving only lends a message. It stays in the queue until a worker acknowledges it.
steps.caption: Worker A holds a 30-second lease on one message.

steps.title: Acknowledge on success
steps.body: Worker A calls the email provider and gets a success reply. Only then does it send an acknowledgement (ack) to the queue, and the ack deletes the message for good. The order matters: ack after the work is done, never before. If the worker acked first and died a moment later, the email would be lost, with no copy left to retry.
steps.idea: An ack means 'done, delete it'. Send it only after the work really succeeded.
steps.caption: Email sent first, then the message is deleted.

steps.title: A worker crashes mid-job
steps.body: Now Worker A sends an email but crashes before it can ack. The queue never hears back. After the 30 second visibility timeout, the message becomes visible again and Worker B receives it as attempt 2. Nothing is lost, which is the good news. The bad news: Worker B sends the email again, so the customer gets two. The sent counter shows it: 801, then 802 (A), then 803 (B's duplicate).
steps.idea: At-least-once delivery means no message is lost, but a message may be handled twice.
steps.caption: No ack arrives, so the message is delivered again.

steps.title: Make consumers idempotent
steps.body: A plain queue cannot promise exactly-once handling, so make handling twice harmless. This is called idempotency. Replay the same crash with a fix: Worker B sends the email with a key such as 'receipt-order-81', and the provider ignores the repeat, so the count stays at 802. If the provider has no such key, check a table of processed keys first. That narrows the gap but cannot be perfectly atomic, so a rare duplicate remains, which is fine for a receipt. Also set the visibility timeout above your slowest normal job.
steps.idea: Pair at-least-once delivery with idempotent workers, and the result is effectively once.
steps.caption: Same crash, but the repeat is ignored.

steps.title: A poison message
steps.body: One message has a malformed email address, so every attempt fails. Retried forever, it would waste capacity and hide real problems. So the queue has a maximum receive count, here 5. After 5 failed deliveries (exact rules vary by broker), the queue moves the message to a dead-letter queue (DLQ), where it waits for a person or a repair job. Redrive means moving parked messages back to the main queue once the bug is fixed. A truly malformed address is a permanent error, so a real worker should fail it fast.
steps.idea: A dead-letter queue parks messages that keep failing, so they stop wasting retries and can be inspected.
steps.caption: After 5 failed tries the message is parked in the DLQ.

steps.title: What the queue bought us
steps.body: Producers write and move on. Workers pull at their own pace, and the queue buffers any gap. Receive lends a message, ack deletes it, and the visibility timeout brings back work from dead workers. That gives at-least-once delivery, so workers must be idempotent. A DLQ catches messages that never succeed, and a growing DLQ or queue depth is your alarm. The 3,000 burst messages end as 2,999 emails sent plus 1 dead letter. A queue gives each message to one worker. If several services each need every message, that is pub/sub, covered next.
steps.idea: Decouple with a queue, ack after success, expect duplicates, and watch the DLQ.
steps.caption: The full path, with a safety net.

quiz.q: A worker receives a message, finishes the job, but crashes just before sending the ack. What happens next with a standard at-least-once queue?
options: The message is lost because the worker died
The message becomes visible again after the visibility timeout and is delivered to a worker again
The queue detects the crash and deletes the message
The producer is told to resend it
quiz.why: Without an ack, the lease simply expires and the message returns to the queue. That is how at-least-once delivery avoids loss, at the cost of possible duplicate processing.

quiz.q: Jobs normally take 20 seconds but sometimes 90 seconds. The visibility timeout is 30 seconds. What is the most likely symptom?
options: Workers will run out of memory
Messages will be dropped silently
Slow jobs will be redelivered to another worker while still running, causing duplicates
The queue will stop accepting new messages
quiz.why: A job that outlasts the lease becomes visible to others while the first worker is still going. Set the timeout above your slowest normal job, or extend the lease while working.

quiz.q: Why should a consumer acknowledge a message only after the work succeeds?
options: Acking early would lose the work if the consumer crashes afterwards
Acks are slow, so they should be delayed
The queue refuses early acks
Late acks prevent duplicates
quiz.why: Ack deletes the message. If you ack first and crash, no copy remains to retry. Acking last trades possible duplicates for no loss.

quiz.q: Your DLQ depth suddenly rises from 0 to 4,000 right after a deploy. What is the best reading?
options: The queue is healthy; the DLQ is just a cache
Producers are sending too fast
The new consumer code probably fails on messages it should handle, so investigate and then redrive the messages
Visibility timeout is too long
quiz.why: Messages typically reach the DLQ after repeated failed attempts. A jump right after a deploy points at a consumer bug, and once it is fixed the parked messages can be moved back to the main queue.

quiz.q: Orders arrive in a 10 second burst at 300/s. Two workers process 40/s each. What does the queue do for you here?
options: It makes the workers faster
It holds the backlog (about 2,200 messages) and lets the workers drain it at their own pace
It rejects messages above 80 per second
It guarantees each email is sent once
quiz.why: A queue buffers the gap between arrival rate and processing rate. It does not speed up consumers or guarantee exactly-once, but the producer is not slowed by the consumers' pace (up to the queue's limits).

cheatsheet.def: The producer writes messages to the queue; the consumer reads and handles them. Neither needs to know the other's speed or whether it is currently running.

Time a received message stays hidden; with no ack it reappears. Set it above your slowest job. Names vary: SQS says visibility timeout, Pub/Sub says ack deadline, RabbitMQ redelivers when the consumer connection drops.
Tells the queue the work is done so the message can be deleted. Send it after success, not before.
Every message is delivered one or more times. Nothing is lost, but duplicates can happen after crashes or timeouts.
Handling the same message twice has the same effect as once, for example by using a dedupe key or an upsert.
Holding area for messages that exceeded the maximum receive count. Alert on its depth, fix the cause, then redrive.
Messages waiting and the age of the oldest one. Rising depth means consumers are too slow or stuck; use it to autoscale workers.
When consumers fall behind, the queue grows. Limit its size or slow producers if the backlog could outlive its usefulness.
